Optimize BtreeRangeIter: lazy right boundary + PageHint::Clean propagation

Two complementary optimizations for range scans:

1. Lazy right boundary for unbounded ranges: When a range scan has an
   unbounded end (e.g., `table.range(key..)`), the previous code eagerly
   traversed the entire B-tree to find the rightmost leaf — work that is
   never needed for forward iteration. The right boundary is now computed
   lazily on the first `next_back()` call only. For forward-only scans this
   saves one full root-to-leaf traversal (~tree depth page reads) per scan.

2. PageHint::Clean propagation: BtreeRangeIter now accepts and stores a
   PageHint, using get_page_extended() throughout. This lets read-only
   iterators skip the write-buffer mutex check on every page access.
   Btree::range() passes self.hint (already PageHint::Clean for read txns).

Measured improvement on the "random range reads" sub-benchmark
(500,000 scans × 10 elements, 5M item database):
  Before: ~2056ms
  After:  ~1860ms
  ~10% faster

Fix restore_savepoint() to always revert changes

state, pending_table_updates still contains modifications staged before

Optimize write performance

Extend in-place deletion threshold from page_size/2 to page_size/3

   When deleting entries from uncommitted B-tree leaf pages, the previous
   code only used the efficient in-place removal path (LeafMutator::remove)
   when the page remained at least 50% full. Below 50% but above the merge
   threshold of 33%, it fell through to a slow path that unnecessarily
   allocated a new page, copied all remaining entries, and freed the old
   page.

   For the benchmark workload (24-byte keys, 150-byte values, ~22 entries
   per leaf), this meant that deletions leaving 8-11 entries (positions
   between 33% and 50% capacity) took the slow path. During bulk deletion
   of 2.575M entries, approximately 379K deletions per leaf traversed this
   unnecessary rebuild path.

   By lowering the threshold to page_size/3 (matching the existing merge
   threshold), all non-merge deletions on uncommitted pages use the
   efficient in-place path. This saves one page allocation, one page
   deallocation, and a full data copy per affected deletion.

Dynamic read/write cache partitioning

Previously the cache budget was statically partitioned: 90% for the read
cache, 10% for the write buffer.  During large write transactions the
dirty-page working set often exceeded the write buffer's 10% allocation,
causing constant eviction of dirty pages to disk followed by re-reading
them on the next in-place modification — an expensive thrashing pattern
dominated by pread/pwrite syscalls.

Replace the static split with dynamic sharing governed by three invariants:

  1. The write buffer never exceeds 50% of the total cache budget.
     Excess pages are flushed to disk immediately.
  2. The write buffer may evict read-cache entries only while
     write < 50% AND read > 50% (fairness).
  3. read + write never exceeds 100% of the budget.

These rules guarantee that the read cache can use up to 100% when no
writes are active, while write-heavy workloads can grow the write buffer
up to 50% without starving readers below 50%.

Enforcement is split across two code paths:

  write() — Two sequential steps:
    (a) If write > 50%, flush write-buffer LRU entries to disk (rule 1).
    (b) After (a), write <= 50%.  If the total still exceeds the budget
        then read must be > 50%, so evict from the read cache (rules 2+3).
        This is done via evict_from_read_cache(), which iterates read-cache
        stripes under the write-buffer mutex (safe because the lock ordering
        is always write_buffer lock → read_cache lock).

  read() — On a cache miss, if read + write > budget, evict one page from
    the local read-cache stripe (rule 3).  The read path cannot evict
    write-buffer entries due to the lock-ordering constraint.

The two usage counters (read_cache_bytes, write_buffer_bytes) are
AtomicUsize; the total is computed on the fly.  A non-atomic read of the
two counters can briefly over- or under-count by one page, but the budget
is a soft limit and the error is self-correcting on the next operation.

Also simplifies the API: Builder, Database::new(), ReadOnlyDatabase::new(),
TransactionalMemory::new(), and PagedCachedFile::new() now pass a single
`cache_size` instead of separate read/write limits.

Skip redundant branch updates

Skip redundant branch updates:
When a child subtree is modified in-place on an uncommitted page, the
child's page number and checksum (DEFERRED) don't change. Previously,
every mutation still called get_page_mut + write_child_page at every
ancestor branch level, writing identical data. Now we detect this case
(new_root == child_page && new_checksum == child_checksum) and return
immediately, cascading the skip up through all branch levels.

During bulk load of 5M random keys (~23 entries/leaf, ~79 children/branch,
tree height 4), this skips ~14.3M redundant branch update operations
(5M inserts × 3 branch levels - 217K first-visit updates). During
removal of 2.5M keys in one transaction, it skips ~7M redundant updates.

Fix data loss in restore_savepoint() by clearing freed_pages

restore_savepoint() did not clear the freed_pages list before
repopulating it from DATA_ALLOCATED_TABLE. When copy-on-write
operations added old pages to freed_pages before the savepoint was
restored, those stale entries persisted. On commit they were written
to DATA_FREED_TABLE, and a subsequent transaction would free pages
still referenced by the committed tree root, causing corruption when
those pages were reallocated.

perf: lazy-size BuddyAllocator bitmaps to reduce memory overhead

Each region's BuddyAllocator pre-allocated its per-order bitmaps at the
full region capacity (up to 1M pages for a 4 GiB region). For small or
just-opened databases, this meant carrying ~256 KB of bitmap data per
region that represents pages that don't yet exist.

Start each bitmap at the actual page count, with the tree pre-padded to
the full region height via new_padded() so resize() never needs to
insert new levels. Growth is handled by the existing resize() path,
amortized O(n) via Vec's doubling.

This extends the same lazy-sizing pattern that was applied to
RegionTracker in #1111 to the BuddyAllocator. On-disk format is
unchanged — serialization has always been based on len, not capacity.

For an in-memory database profiled with DHAT, this reduces resident
bitmap memory from ~1.6 MB to ~63 KB per database.

Fix panic in delete_table() when the table was modified in the same txn

delete_table() walked the table tree and unconditionally pushed every page
into freed_pages, which is later written into DATA_FREED_TABLE on commit. That
list must contain only committed pages, since committed-but-orphaned pages get
freed by a later process_freed_pages() pass (and uncommitted pages allocated
by the current transaction are tracked separately in DATA_ALLOCATED_TABLE for
savepoint restoration).

When a table was modified earlier in the same transaction, copy-on-write
allocated new uncommitted leaf and branch pages. delete_table()'s walk reached
those pages and added them to freed_pages, violating the invariant. On commit
this triggers a debug_assert in store_data_freed_pages() and aborts the
transaction; in release builds the same page would end up in both
DATA_FREED_TABLE and DATA_ALLOCATED_TABLE.

Fix by mirroring how retain_in() and BtreeExtractIf's Drop impl handle this:
release uncommitted pages immediately via free_if_uncommitted() and only push
committed pages into freed_pages. Collect the pages from the visit before
freeing, since free_if_uncommitted() invalidates the page cache and the
recursive walk in visit_all_pages() reads each page to discover its children.

Fix page leak when aborting a transaction that created a persistent savepoint

abort_inner() previously called delete_persistent_savepoint() for each id in
created_persistent_savepoints. That only queues the deallocation into
deleted_persistent_savepoints, which is drained by commit_inner() - a path
abort_inner() never runs. rollback_uncommitted_writes() reverses the
on-disk SAVEPOINT_TABLE / NEXT_SAVEPOINT_TABLE mutations, but the savepoint
stays alive in the in-memory TransactionTracker: valid_savepoints keeps the
SavepointId and live_read_transactions still holds its refcount.

That ghost savepoint pins oldest_live_read_transaction to an old transaction
id for the rest of the database's lifetime, so process_freed_pages() stops
reclaiming pages in every later commit. Each subsequent write transaction
that modifies the data permanently leaks its freed pages.

perf: avoid Vec->Arc copy and other allocation hygiene in page_store

Several small allocation fixes in the page cache and bitmap
serialization paths. No behavior change — all outputs are identical.

PagedCachedFile page buffers (cached_file.rs)

  vec![0; len].into() and read_direct(..).into() each allocated a

  `Arc::new_uninit_slice` (stable since 1.82):
    - zero_filled_arc(len): zero-filled Arc<[u8]>
    - read_direct_into_arc(offset, len): fills the Arc by delegating
      to StorageBackend::read, which contractually writes every byte
      or returns Err

  allocation volume (~17.6 MB of churn saved across the run).

BuddyAllocator::to_vec (buddy_allocator.rs)

  Each BtreeBitmap was serialized twice — once to measure its length
  (to write the offset header), then again to copy into the output.
  Serialize once into a Vec<Vec<u8>>, compute sizes from there, then
  write the result into a pre-sized Vec<u8>.

U64GroupedBitmap::{to_vec,from_bytes} (bitmap.rs)

InMemoryBackend::set_len (backends.rs)

  Replace `reserve(n) + push(0)` loop with `resize(len, 0)` — idiomatic
  single memset instead of a push-per-byte loop.

Fix bug in restore_savepoint() when durability is not Immediate

restore_savepoint() applied its in-memory reverts (tree root, DATA_FREED_TABLE
extraction, allocated_pages, freed_pages, tracker invalidation) before calling
delete_persistent_savepoint() for any persistent savepoints whose id was
greater than the restored one. delete_persistent_savepoint() returns
Err(InvalidSavepoint) when durability != Immediate, at which point the reverts
had already been applied but were not rolled back. A caller who ignored the
error and committed durably persisted the reverted tree root, silently
discarding every write made between the savepoint and the current transaction.

Validate the durability precondition upfront so restore_savepoint() fails
before mutating any state when it cannot complete.

Fix aborting restore_savepoint()

Aborting a transaction in which restore_savepoint() had been called
could leave more recent savepoints invalid and/or leak database space

restore_savepoint() invalidates every savepoint whose id is strictly
greater than the restored savepoint's id so that the user cannot later
try to restore one "on another timeline". Previously that invalidation
eagerly mutated the shared TransactionTracker::valid_savepoints map.
rollback_uncommitted_writes() reverts the on-disk SAVEPOINT_TABLE
changes but not that in-memory map edit, and the
deleted_persistent_savepoints queue is dropped on abort without
running deallocate_savepoint, so live_read_transactions retained a
reference for every "ghost" savepoint that was still present on disk.

The concrete leak follows from store_allocated_pages()'s purge loop,
which walks oldest_savepoint() to decide how much of DATA_ALLOCATED_TABLE
to drop. With the ghost savepoint removed from valid_savepoints but
still on disk, a subsequent deletion of the user-known savepoint leaves
valid_savepoints empty. Every later commit then purges
DATA_ALLOCATED_TABLE up to u64::MAX, discarding the allocation history
of any transactions that happened after the on-disk savepoint was
created. When that savepoint is eventually restored (for example, after
a database reopen re-registers it), restore_savepoint() no longer has
the allocation records it needs to move those pages into freed_pages,
so they remain allocated but unreachable from the restored tree root -
an unbounded leak proportional to the number of intervening write
transactions.

Fix by making the invalidation fully transactional:

* TransactionTracker gains a read-only list_savepoints_after() and a
  batch invalidate_savepoints(); the old invalidate_savepoints_after()
  (which mutated on the spot) is removed.
* WriteTransaction carries a per-transaction invalidated_savepoints
  set. restore_savepoint() populates it from list_savepoints_after()
  without touching the shared map. Subsequent checks in
  restore_savepoint() consult both the tracker's is_valid_savepoint
  and this set, so a savepoint that was invalidated earlier in the
  same transaction still cannot be restored.
* commit_inner() applies the invalidation to the shared map by calling
  invalidate_savepoints() after deleted_persistent_savepoints has been
  drained. abort_inner() simply clears the set, so the shared tracker
  is never left out of sync with on-disk state.

Keeping the shared map untouched until commit also means that an
ephemeral Savepoint whose handle is dropped between restore() and
abort() cleans up through its existing Drop path (which decrements
live_read_transactions and removes the valid_savepoints entry) without
any interaction with a stale stashed list.

The existing small_pages2 test encoded the buggy behavior (asserting
savepoint4 was still invalid after an aborted restore); update it to
match, and add restore_savepoint_abort_unbounded_leak plus
restore_savepoint_abort_after_ephemeral_drop as regression tests.

Consolidate WriteTransaction savepoint lifecycle state

The three independent mutexes (`created_persistent_savepoints`,
`deleted_persistent_savepoints`, `invalidated_savepoints`) on
WriteTransaction have been the source of a long tail of bugs
(5d65045, 44a9ff5, 75bf290, 19f77ab, 4550d5a) because the commit and
abort paths touch them asymmetrically across multiple functions - every
new piece of state added another opportunity to forget one of the paths.

Replace them with a single `SavepointTransactionState` struct that owns
all three fields and exposes `apply_on_commit` / `apply_on_abort`
methods. Both methods consume the state, and they are defined adjacent
so a reviewer can see the complete commit/abort contract in one place.
Adding a new piece of savepoint-lifecycle state now requires a single
struct-field edit plus the two symmetric apply methods, rather than
threading a new mutex through `commit_inner`, `abort_inner`,
`set_durability`, and `restore_savepoint`.

No behavior change: the existing savepoint regression tests (unbounded
leak on abort, partial-revert-as-data-loss, stale freed_pages, foreign
database panic, ephemeral-drop-after-abort) continue to pass.

Avoid copying keys in leaf overwrite paths

AccessGuardMut::insert previously copied the existing key into a Vec on
every value replacement so that the borrow on the page could be released
before LeafMutator::new reborrowed the page mutably. The copy was only
needed to satisfy the lifetime; LeafMutator::insert with overwrite=true
never read the key bytes -- only key.len() was used.

Split LeafMutator::insert into insert (true inserts) and replace (value
replacement), and the corresponding space-check helpers. The replace
path takes no key argument and derives the required delta from the
existing value length, which eliminates the copy and simplifies the
control flow by dropping the overwrite flag.

Updated all call sites: AccessGuardMut::insert, btree_mutator in-place
fast path, insert_inplace_helper, and both multimap_table overwrite
sites. The finalize_tree_and_subtree_checksums path also loses an
entry.key().to_vec() since replace no longer needs the key.

Avoid allocating a page for a branch that will be immediately merged

During deletion, when a branch ends up less than 33% full, the result was
returned as `PartialBranch(page_number, ...)`. The parent branch then reads
that page back via a `BranchAccessor` and rebuilds it merged with a sibling,
so the page allocation and its immediate conditional_free were pure waste.

Hold `PartialBranch` in its unbuilt form (owned children + keys) so the
caller can merge directly without a round trip through the page allocator.
The root-level handler in `delete()` now builds the page itself, which is
the only path that still needs a real page for a partial branch.

Require callers of get_page to provide a PageHint

Previously, get_page had a convenience wrapper that defaulted to
PageHint::None, forcing every read to take the write_buffer lock
even when the caller knew the page was clean (e.g. read transactions).
Making the hint mandatory surfaces this decision at every call site,
so read-only paths can propagate PageHint::Clean end-to-end and skip
the extra locking, while write-path callers keep PageHint::None.

verify_checksum, AllPageNumbersBtreeIter) now take a hint parameter
or store it alongside the tree, so the decision is made once at the
top-level transaction boundary rather than silently lost inside a
helper.

Optimize pop_first / pop_last to run in a single tree descent

Table::pop_first / pop_last used to build a full BtreeRangeIter over the
unbounded range `..`, pull a single entry out of it, copy the key, drop
the iterator, and then call remove() which re-descended the tree. The
iterator construction allocated cursor state that was immediately
discarded, and for pop_last the left-side descent was pure overhead
(the right-side lookup happens lazily on next_back()).

Collapse this into one walk. Introduce a DeleteTarget { Key, First, Last }
enum and parameterize the delete helpers on it. In branch nodes, First
picks child 0 and Last picks the last child, so we reach the leaf without
needing the key. At the leaf, for First / Last we hand back an
AccessGuard<K> for the deleted key alongside the value AccessGuard. In the
two deletion paths that don't hold a mutable page reference, the key guard
shares the same Arc / PageImpl backing as the value, so no key copy is
needed; only the in-place remove_on_drop path still copies the key, since
its value guard owns the mutable page and mutates it on drop.

The normal delete() path is unchanged behaviorally; it just threads a
None key-capture slot through. Microbenchmark of 50k sequential pops
(64B values):

  pop_first: ~70ms -> ~38ms  (~1.8x faster)
  pop_last:  ~80ms -> ~39ms  (~2.0x faster)

Full redb_benchmark (bulk insert / random reads / 2.5M row remove) is
unchanged within measurement noise.

Reclaim unpersisted pages across savepoints in non-durable commits

Non-durable commits previously clamped free_until_transaction to the
oldest savepoint in process_freed_pages_nondurable(). The clamp existed
because DATA_FREED_TABLE edits made by the non-durable path were not
mirrored into DATA_ALLOCATED_TABLE, so freeing an unpersisted page across
a savepoint would leave a stale allocation record that savepoint restore
would later re-queue, causing a double-free.

Track the allocation records for unpersisted data-tree pages in memory
(TransactionalMemory::unpersisted_allocations) instead of writing them to
DATA_ALLOCATED_TABLE. free_if_unpersisted() and free() now remove the
reclaimed page from that map, so the record stays consistent with the
allocator. Durable commits flush the map to DATA_ALLOCATED_TABLE (after
process_freed_pages, so pages reclaimed during the commit are excluded)
and savepoint restore iterates both DATA_ALLOCATED_TABLE and the
in-memory map. With these invariants the clamp is unnecessary and
unpersisted pages can be reclaimed immediately even when a savepoint
exists, dramatically reducing the work that restore_savepoint() and
subsequent non-durable commits have to do.

Fix issue #1165: compact() could grow the file on drop

Database::compact() trims the file with ShrinkPolicy::Maximum, which on
a densely packed database leaves the region with zero free pages. When
Database::drop subsequently runs a quick_repair commit to update
ALLOCATOR_STATE_TABLE, the commit is forced to call grow() to obtain
pages for the system-table write. After the commit, try_shrink() cannot
reclaim the growth: grow()'s trailing free blocks are buddy-aligned at
high page positions, and the default alloc() splits those blocks,
landing the commit's allocations at high absolute pages and leaving
trailing_free = 0. The net effect is that the file doubles after
compact() -- matching the 17 MB -> 33 MB growth in the issue.

Remove redundant third commit in Database::compact()

Each iteration of the compaction loop ran three commits: one to relocate
high pages (compact_pages), one to drain DATA_FREED_TABLE and shrink, and
a third that the TODO described as defensive, in case modifying a system
table during the second commit left more pending frees behind.

transactions.rs:

  - process_freed_pages(free_until=T3) extracts every sub-T3 entry from
    DATA_FREED_TABLE. The old btree pages it sheds are system-tree pages
    and accumulate in the system_tables freed_pages Vec (system_freed_pages).
  - compact() calls set_two_phase_commit(true) but never set_quick_repair,
    so the quick-repair branch at transactions.rs:1706-1743 is skipped and
    store_system_freed_pages() is not called. SYSTEM_FREED_TABLE stays
    empty (its root is None).
  - After self.mem.commit() returns, the unconditional drain loop at
    transactions.rs:1758-1762 empties system_freed_pages by calling
    self.mem.free() on every page. Per the comment there, this is safe
    because those pages are only reachable from write transactions, which
    are serialized by the &mut self on compact().

So by the time control returns to compact():
  - DATA_FREED_TABLE's root is None (all entries extracted).
  - SYSTEM_FREED_TABLE's root is None (never written to).
  - The in-memory allocator already reflects the system-tree frees, so
    the next transaction's try_shrink sees them.

That matches the post-condition pending_free_pages() checks, which is
why the assert!(!txn.pending_free_pages()?) holds with two commits. The
third commit adds no state transitions - it just rewrites the same
system root with the same shrink policy.

An ephemeral Savepoint can be dropped from a different thread than the one
committing the WriteTransaction that created it, since WriteTransaction is

transactions. A savepoint is also a live read, so absent concurrency the two

Distinguish composite types of user types from built-in composites

A composite type (`Option`, `Vec`, tuple, or array) built its `TypeName`
from only the inner type's name string, discarding the inner type's

classification byte exists precisely to keep a user type named "u32"
from colliding with the built-in `u32`, but that protection was lost one
nesting level down.

is now itself classified user-defined, keeping the same name string.
Composites of only built-in types are byte-for-byte unchanged, so
existing databases open unchanged.

non-bubbled classification. To keep them readable, TypeName carries an
in-memory-only record of the classification it was bubbled from (never
serialized), and check_match accepts that prior spelling in addition to
the current one. For fixed-width composites the prior spelling is

still correctly rejected rather than silently misread. A flat
user-defined type records no such classification, so this never lets a
user type named "u32" alias the built-in `u32` at the top level.

fix: prevent infinite recursion (stack overflow) on cyclic page corruption

During database startup/recovery or integrity checks on a corrupted redb file,
B-tree tree-walking operations could get stuck in an infinite recursion,
eventually exhausting the call stack and crashing the application.

This was occurring in two main recursive operations:
1. RawBtree::verify_checksum_helper: Recursing down branch children to verify leaf checksums.
2. UntypedBtree::visit_pages_helper: Recursing down branch children to visit pages.

If page corruption introduces cyclic pointers (e.g., a child page number points
to an ancestor page), these functions would loop indefinitely.

This commit resolves the issue by introducing cycle detection:
- In RawBtree::verify_checksum_helper, we track the active DFS traversal path via a visited stack (Vec<PageNumber>). If a page has already been visited in the active path, it returns Ok(false) (checksum verification failure) instead of looping, allowing standard database repair/rollback to recover or fail gracefully.
- In UntypedBtree::visit_pages_helper, we verify if a child page is already part of the active path (path.parents() or current page_number). If a cycle is detected, it returns a StorageError::Corrupted error.

Added unit tests:
- test_page_path_cycle_detection to verify loop detection on PagePaths.
- test_verify_checksum_cycle_detection to verify loop detection on active verify stacks.

Recompute root table counts during repair

The number of entries in a btree is stored in its BtreeHeader, next to the
root page number rather than inside the tree, so the page checksums that
verify the tree say nothing about it. For the data and system roots that
BtreeHeader lives in the commit slot, where the slot checksum covers it --
but only as long as a slot that fails verification stays failed. Before
"Preserve torn commit slot bytes during recovery", recovery re-serialized
such a slot with a freshly computed checksum, laundering whatever the torn
bytes decoded to. A count laundered that way is indistinguishable from one
redb wrote, so it survives open, reads, and check_integrity(), and is first
noticed when the tree is next mutated: it reaches the assertion in
MutateHelper::finish_deletion. For the system root that happens on the
commit every Database::drop makes, to remove the allocator state table --
a panic raised while dropping, which aborts outright if the thread is
already unwinding.

Repair is the only place a root enters the system without having been
written by a btree operation that maintained its count, so recompute both
counts there, in rebuild_allocator_state, from the trees it already walks.
Roots that need recounting compare unequal to the stored ones, so
check_integrity() reports the database as repaired rather than clean and
commits the corrected roots, and a repair during open commits them too.
A live non-durable commit whose count disagrees with its tree is rolled
back instead, since only a durable root can be rewritten from there.

This keeps the count an invariant everywhere else: the btree code can go on
trusting it, rather than having every arithmetic operation on it turn
fallible.

Fixes https://github.com/cberner/redb/issues/1303

Refuse writes after a failed integrity check

check_integrity() rebuilds the allocator state: clear_cache_and_reload()
discards the one in memory, because it described the layout from before the
reload, and the repair that follows repopulates it. A failure anywhere in
between leaves no allocator state at all, or one holding only the pages the
walk reached before it stopped -- neither of which describes the file.

The database stayed usable in that state. Every durable commit frees pages,
so the next write ran the allocation paths against it: with no allocator
state the free path hit the assertion guarding it, and with a partial one it
would allocate over pages that are still live. Database::drop makes such a
commit unconditionally, to write the allocator state table, so a caller that
did nothing but check a corrupt file and drop it got a panic raised while
dropping -- an abort, if the thread was already unwinding.

Discard the allocator state on every failure path of the check, so that
having one always means it describes the file, and require one wherever that
matters: beginning a write transaction, re-running the check, and recording
a clean shutdown, which asserts that the in-memory state matched the file.
The commit in Database::drop then reports the failure through its existing
warning path. Reads are unaffected, since they do not allocate.

Keep the database open while a write transaction is live

Database::drop makes a commit to write the allocator state table, which
begins a write transaction. That blocks until the live write transaction
ends, so dropping a Database while one of its WriteTransactions was
alive deadlocked: in the common single-threaded case -- beginning a
transaction and returning it from the function that owns the Database --
it hung forever, since the transaction can only end after drop returns.

Closing immediately instead would break the transaction's contract: it
holds uncommitted work, and its commit() would fail at a distance
because an unrelated handle was dropped. Nor can the transaction be
aborted from Database::drop: rollback requires that no dirty-page
borrows exist (open tables, access guards), and only the transaction's
owner can guarantee that.

Defer the close instead: Database::drop, on finding a live write
transaction, logs a warning, stores the closing responsibility in the
TransactionTracker, and returns without blocking. The transaction
remains fully usable, and when it ends -- by commit, abort, or drop --
releasing the write slot returns the deferred close, which runs at that
point: the allocator state table commit, so that the next open does not
require a repair, and the backend close, which releases the file lock.
The handoff happens under the tracker lock that guards the write slot,
so exactly one of the two sides performs the close, and by the time the
transaction ends no Database handle exists, so the shutdown's own write
transaction cannot block. Read transactions are unaffected: they are
still invalidated when the database closes, just at the deferred point.

Fixes https://github.com/cberner/redb/issues/1072

Poison the database when a commit fails part way

A WriteTransaction::commit() that stops part way -- by error or panic --
can leave the in-memory page allocator inconsistent with the durable
state: process_freed_pages() returns pending-free pages to the allocator
before the new roots are installed, so on failure the freed-table
entries naming those pages remain reachable from the unchanged durable
roots. Backend I/O errors are already latched by CheckedBackend, but a
non-I/O error (e.g. StorageError::Corrupted raised while reading a page
during the commit) left the database writable: the next commit would
process the same freed-table entries again and double-free the pages,
handing them out to two owners and corrupting committed data. A clean
shutdown could then persist the inconsistent allocator state.

Discard the allocator state whenever commit_inner() does not complete,
on both the error and the unwind path. Subsequent begin_write() calls
fail while reads remain available, the shutdown path no longer records
a clean shutdown, and reopening the database rebuilds a consistent
allocator state via repair. begin_write() re-checks the I/O latch and
allocator state after acquiring the write slot, since a waiter can be
woken by the failing commit itself. invalidate_allocator_state()
tolerates poisoned locks, because it also runs while unwinding from a
panic, but leaves the poison set so later accesses stay fail-stop.

Fix stats() walking stale table roots while a table is open

A write transaction learns a table's root only when the table handle is
closed, staging it in pending_table_updates until commit. Reopening the
table and modifying it frees pages reachable from that staged root, and
because they were allocated by this same transaction they return to the
allocator immediately and may be recycled for unrelated tables.
WriteTransaction::stats() preferred the staged root unconditionally, so
calling it while such a table was open walked recycled pages: garbage
statistics in release builds, and with debug_assertions an internal
assertion failure that poisons the tables mutex and then aborts the
process when the open table's destructor panics on the poisoned lock.

stats() now skips the staged root for tables that are currently open and
walks the committed root instead, which cannot be recycled during the
transaction: an open table is reported as of the start of the
transaction, and its in-progress contents are included once it is
closed. This matches the other pending-update walkers (compaction's
relocate_tables and highest_index_pages), which only run without open
tables.

Optimize inserting past the last key in a table

Loading in ascending key order splits the rightmost leaf evenly and then
never returns to it, so half of every leaf left behind is stranded. The
tree can see that this is happening without being told: an insert is past
the last key in the table when every branch of the descent took its last
child and the key sorts after the leaf's last pair.

When it is, and the pair no longer fits, skip the split entirely: leave
the full leaf exactly as it is, and give the new pair a leaf of its own.
That also avoids rebuilding and freeing a page whose contents were not
changing.

Loading 1M pairs, of a 16 byte key and a 150 byte value, in key order now
uses 43,479 leaf pages rather than 83,333, and 91% of the table is data
rather than 47%. Loading the same pairs in random order is unchanged.

The machinery for the cursor API discussed in #1317, gated behind a new

the cursor position never moves, the invariant the coalescing-run
machinery already relies on. A failed splice poisons the cursor:
inserts already reported to the caller were lost, so the transaction
must not commit.

eight threads instead of scaling.

Rename the concurrency modes

ConcurrencyMode named its variants by process count, which was only half true
of the default: SingleProcess admitted one writer, or any number of read-only
handles, because a writer takes the whole-file lock exclusively and readers take
it shared. The design doc's separate "Immutable" mode was that read-only face,
described as a lock protocol of its own.

The variants now name the regime a writer operates under -- ExclusiveWriter,
SingleWriter and MultiWriter -- and whether a handle writes is chosen by open()
against open_read_only(), not by the mode. That separates the sharing regime
from the handle's access, as SQL Server's SINGLE_USER/MULTI_USER against
READ_ONLY and .NET's FileShare against FileAccess do; the whole-file behavior
itself is what bbolt and DuckDB do under a read-only open, and SingleWriter and
MultiWriter follow HDF5's SWMR and BerkeleyDB's CDS and TDS.

The design doc folds Immutable into the exclusive writer section, and the
"immutable byte" becomes the "whole-file reader byte": a byte read-only
exclusive-writer handles hold, as part of their whole-file lock, that a
multi-writer open must probe because such handles leave the shared writer byte
free. The lock layout is unchanged, and so is every handle's behavior.
